Beállítom Robbanószer is volt azon a rejtélyes drónon, amelyet Lipcse repülőterén találtak, miközben a DHL éppen felszálló csomagszállító gépe egy másik ismeretlen tárggyal ütközött szerdára virradó éjjel – írta a BBC. A gépnek nem esett baja, leszálláskor csak kisebb sérülések nyoma látszódott az orrán. Hogy milyen tárggyal ütközött, azt nem tudni. A német rendőrség azt azonban megállapította, hogy a kifutónál talált drónon robbanószer volt. A gyanú szerint a szerkezetet orosz ügynök juttathatta be a repülőtérre. A drónról a tűzszerészek eltávolították a detonátort, amelyet biztonságos körülmények között felrobbantottak. Ukrajna berlini nagykövete szerint nem állhat más a rejtélyes drón mögött, mint Oroszország, amelyhez már több drónos zavarkeltést kötnek a nyugat-európai légtérben. Skip next section India distances itself from Eiffel Tower row over Hindu group's visit 09/09/2026 September 9, 2026 India distances itself from Eiffel Tower row over Hindu group's visit The Eiffel Tower reopened to the public a day after the staff strike Image: Sarah Meyssonnier/REUTERS India's Ministry of External Affairs on Tuesday distanced itself from the controversy arising from Hindu group Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha's (BAPS) visit to the Eiffel Tower. BAPS had earlier apologized after the Eiffel Tower closed Monday when staff went on strike over allegations that female workers were sidelined during a visit by roughly 100 members of the organization. "As to the particular issue pertaining to the Tower, this is a matter purely between the entities concerned," MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said during a press briefing, confirming India was aware of the controversy following BAPS's inauguration of France's first traditional Hindu temple near Paris on Sunday. Jaiswal also addressed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's virtual address at the temple's opening, calling it standard practice for the government to convey "good wishes" on such occasions and saying there was "no cause for any comment" on the matter, local media reported. BAPS said the visit had been pre-coordinated with the tower's operators and that, to its knowledge, no one was denied access, though it apologized to anyone "hurt or inconvenienced." Read more about the controversy here . https://p.dw.com/p/5MJ54 Skip next section Baby orangutans rescued, sparking international smuggling probe 09/09/2026 September 9, 2026 Baby orangutans rescued, sparking international smuggling probe Indian forest officials rescued five baby orangutans in the eastern state of Odisha on Tuesday, with authorities suspecting the great apes were smuggled into the country from Southeast Asia. The animals, not native to India , were found in a forest in the Balasore district. Local legislator Goutam Buddha Das told The Telegraph newspaper that villagers first spotted the orangutans dangling from a tree and initially mistook them for monkeys, before alerting forest officials that their appearance didn't match. He said the area's coastal location suggested the animals could have arrived by sea from Indonesia. "I demand a high-level inquiry to find out who is involved in the racket," Das said. Balasore forest officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar said the three male and two female orangutans were examined by veterinarians, found to be in good health, and given food and oral rehydration solution before being transferred to Nandan Kanan Zoo in Bhubaneswar for quarantine. Odisha Environment Minister Ram Singh Khuntia said the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau is now investigating how the animals reached India . "We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this," he told the IANS news agency. Authorities are also examining whether the animals were destined for sale to buyers in Kolkata. Orangutans are native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. Only about 104,000 remain in the wild, according to the World Wildlife Fund, down from more than 230,000 a century ago. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP Melbourne Imams’ council condemns Melbourne Islamic preacher’s call to ‘take up arms’ against enemies Independent MP Allegra Spender says the comments reinforce the need for stronger protection against hate speech Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Adeshola Ore Community affairs reporter Tue 29 Sep 2026 07.04 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 07.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Australia’s peak body for imams says it is “deeply concerned” about reports a Melbourne-based Islamic preacher called for followers to “take up arms against his enemies” and not take “Jews and the Christians for friends”. The Australian National Imams’ Council (ANIC) released a statement on Tuesday after Nine newspapers revealed the preacher who goes by the name Abu Ahmad made the comments during a sermon in July. Reading from a book chapter, Ahmad said Muslims should not “take the Jews and the Christians for friends” in a video posted to the social media feed of Melbourne-based Al Bayyinah Islamic Centre in July. “For the sake of Allah, it includes the obligation to declare enmity for his sake, opposition for the sake of Allah. It is to declare opposition, indeed, to take up arms against his enemies, to shun them, and to stay far from them both in word and deed. This proves that simple opposition of the spirit is not enough and that it must be complete by honouring of your commitment,” he said. “If the aim of the enemies of Islam, whether they are atheists, or Jews, or Christians, or modernists, or Zionists, or communists, is the emasculation of … the Muslims and the erosion of their unique character in order to make them the ass of the chosen people, as it is put in the protocols of the elders of Zion , then the urgency of this issue should become clear to every Muslim,” he said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email In an Instagram post on Monday, the Al Bayyinah Islamic Centre included a statement from the preacher . “The statements the article is attributing to me were from a passage of a book that I was reading during a lesson on al-Walāʾ wal-Barāʾ. They were not a personal call from me for Muslims to attack Christians, Jews or other non-Muslims,” the post signed off by Ahmad said. The post attached a video which he said was an “explanation of that very passage from the same lesson” and explained it “does not permit harming, oppressing or being unjust towards peaceful non-Muslims. “Unfortunately, quoting the book without including the explanation that followed gives a completely different impression of what was being taught,” the post said. ANIC said it “strongly and unequivocally condemns any call by any religious or non-religious preacher, leader or individual to take up arms against civilians, religious communities or the Australian people”. ANIC said it would not make findings about the “individual or the precise context of the reported remarks” until it could properly review material. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion ANIC reiterated it “categorically rejects incitement to violence, hatred or harm against any person or community”. “The safety, security and wellbeing of Australia and the Australian people are fundamental responsibilities that Australian Muslims, Imams and religious leaders must uphold. Islamic teachings require Muslims to honour the sanctity of human life, fulfil their responsibilities to society and contribute positively to the communities and country in which they live.” The peak body called on all religious leaders, regardless of faith, to exercise responsibility in their public statements. It added that the alleged conduct of an individual should not be used to condemn or blame an entire faith or community. The Albanese government was forced to abandon anti-vilification laws that would have given authorities greater powers to crack down on religious leaders who promote hatred on the basis of religions, race, gender or sexuality after it failed to gain support from the Nationals and the Greens. On Tuesday, the independent federal MP Allegra Spender told Nine newspapers the comments showed “why we needed stronger and nationally consistent hate speech legislation”. Photograph: Zsolt Szigetváry/EPA View image in fullscreen Hungary's prime minister, Péter Magyar, speaks at an extraordinary session of the national assembly, during which deputies voted to suspend his immunity, in Budapest, Hungary, 28 September 2026. Photograph: Zsolt Szigetváry/EPA Hungary Two ex-ministers from Orbán era held over suspected bribery and misuse of public funds Ministers from former far-right government arrested after MPs vote to lift their immunity Jon Henley Europe correspondent Tue 29 Sep 2026 08.09 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 10.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two ministers in Viktor Orbán’s former far-right government suspected separately of misusing millions of euros of public funds and taking millions more in bribes have been detained, hours after Hungarian MPs voted to lift their immunity. Prosecutors said on Tuesday that Balázs Hankó, Orbán’s culture minister and still an MP in the former prime minister’s nationalist Fidesz party, was ​taken into custody late on Monday. Hankó is suspected of misappropriation of funds. He has denied any wrongdoing. Miklós Seszták, an MP from Fidesz ally KDNP who served as minister for national development between 2014 and 2018, was also detained on Monday as part of an ⁠investigation into alleged bribery. He too has denied wrongdoing. “Yesterday was an important day,” said Hungary’s prime minister, Péter Magyar on Tuesday. His Tisza party swept to victory in April elections promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of office during Orbán’s 16-year rule. “After decades of lies, for the first time, many millions of Hungarians could experience what real regime change and equality before the law really mean, Magyar said on social media . “Hungary is no longer a country without consequences.” The arrests came hours after Hungary’s parliament on Monday voted to suspend Hankó and Seszták’s immunity – but also that of Magyar, who had asked for his to be lifted so he could clear himself of what he called a “character assassination”. The graft investigations into the Orbán-era ministers are the first against senior figures in the former government. Magyar, meanwhile, is accused of snatching a phone from a man filming him in a nightclub in 2024 and throwing it into the Danube River. The prime minister has denied his conduct amounted to theft and called the case, which involves a damages claim of €300 (£260), a “sham”. He said he took responsibility for his actions but denied committing a crime and criticised prosecutors for “conflating” the ex-ministers’ corruption cases with “an attempted political character assassination”. Magyar ​has repeatedly said that in recent years corruption and misuse of public funds have cost Hungary between 8% and 10% of its GDP under successive governments led by Orbán, who has repeatedly denied allowing rampant corruption and outright theft of public money during more than a decade and half in power. Prosecutors allege Hankó oversaw the criminal misuse of 17.3bn forints (€47m) of public funds from Hungary’s national cultural fund (NKA), channelling the money to artists and groups with ties to Fidesz and financing its 2026 election campaign. “My conscience is clear, this is a political show trial,” Hankó said ‌in a live video broadcast on Orbán’s Facebook page shortly before his arrest. In July, police raided the Fidesz offices and seized the party’s internet servers in connection ⁠with alleged “misappropriation and other criminal offences” at the NKA, prompting Orbán to accuse authorities of conducting a sham investigation in order to render his party “legally unviable”. Prosecutors also suspect Seszták of accepting more than 12bn forints (€32.6m) in bribes and kickbacks connected to vehicle procurements under Hungary’s state bus company, as well as to public construction projects. The case centres on the purchase of secondhand buses at allegedly inflated prices. Separately, Hungary’s national ‌asset protection and recovery office, the anti-corruption body established by Magyar’s government as part of his anti-graft ⁠drive, on ⁠Monday announced the ​first four cases it intends to tackle. The first concerned “selling ​political connections to obtain residence permits ‌for employment”, the body said in a statement, and the second case is about alleged corruption involving local council expenditure on park maintenance and public catering. The third case involved “a state-owned company and state investments” and has links to Dániel Jellinek , a real estate mogul and one of Hungary’s wealthiest businessmen, the statement said. The real estate firm that Jellinek heads has said he will cooperate fully with the authorities. “Our firm position is that Mr Jellinek has not committed any offence in connection with the matter. We are confident that the investigation will confirm this and that the proceedings against him will soon be discontinued,” it said in a statement this month. The fourth concerned “seemingly unjustified propaganda ​and event costs” at the sovereignty protection office , ​an Orbán-era body set up to monitor what Fidesz alleged was “undue political interference” by foreign entities in Hungary, and abolished by Magyar’s government in June. Photograph: Ange/Alamy Health Majority of Australians who report penicillin allergy not truly allergic Peak body for immunologists changes guidelines as evidence shows up to 90% of those reporting allergy don’t have one Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Jack Larkin Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 15.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The majority of Australians who report a penicillin allergy are not truly allergic, prompting the peak body for immunologists to change its guidelines in a bid to reduce hospital stays and tackle antimicrobial resistance. Penicillin, one of the most commonly prescribed antibiotics in Australia, was thought to cause allergies in 10% of Australians, or about 2.8 million people. But the latest evidence shows up to 90% of those reporting a penicillin allergy do not have one. Australian researchers identify new subtype of depression linked to body clock disruptions Read more The changes to the Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy guidelines, which have been published in the Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology , give the first peer-reviewed and updated advice to GPs and other health professionals about how to diagnose and manage the allergy, and when to refer to a specialist. Prof Michaela Lucas, a clinical immunologist, said misdiagnosis occurs for a number of reasons, with people sometimes experiencing a rash or nausea after taking penicillin and assuming it is an allergy, or doctors wanting to be cautious and recording side effects as allergies. Other people were told by a parent that they suffered a reaction when they were a child and carry that diagnosis through to adulthood without questioning it, she said, while some side effects may also be due to the illness itself and not the medicine. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Penicillin is an important antibiotic option, as it treats common infections, said Lucas, a professor at the University of Western Australia’s medical school. “It is also what is known as a narrow spectrum antibiotic, which means it is targeted at the bug specifically causing the infection,” she said. “Once you have to avoid narrow classes of drugs, you have to use broader spectrum antibiotics which have a bigger impact of your gut microbiome as they are associated with also killing good bacteria and allowing superbugs to come in and take residency.” Superbugs are strains of bacteria that are highly resistant to multiple standard treatments. “Antimicrobial resistance matters beyond the individual patient, because resistant bacteria can spread between people and through communities,” Lucas said. “If someone develops a serious infection that is resistant to several antibiotics, doctors can be left with very limited treatment options.” Dr Nick Cooling, the chair of the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners’ allergy special interest group, said the guidelines were based on the latest evidence, and a consensus report from a range of medical specialities. He hopes the guidance will cut health costs in the community and ease the burden on immunologists. “We know that people who have a penicillin allergy label go to hospital more,” he said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “They spend longer in hospital, and they also cost the system more.” This is because of more treatments needing to be trialled, side-effects from those treatments, and delays in finding alternative treatments. “The ability to clarify that with these patients will reduce hospital costs but also the whole health system cost,” he said. “We need all health professionals to be involved in this because if we’re going to de-label some 2.8 million people in Australia, you can’t just rely on the 300 immunologists to do that.” Cooling urged affected patients to raise the question of a penicillin allergy with their GP, and with cases where the potential risk of harm is low, doctors could give their patient penicillin and monitor for symptoms. But he warned: “No one should try taking penicillin themselves to find out whether they are allergic. Antibiotics should only be taken when prescribed for the individual taking them.” For Tammy Prescino, the issue of penicillin allergy is a very real concern. She welcomes the changes, with her 70-year-old mother and 12-year-old daughter both diagnosed. Prescino worries that if her mother were to get an infection she could miss out on the benefits of penicillin. She plans to see a doctor and to get her family reassessed. “Because if she doesn’t have the penicillin allergy, then we wouldn’t have to withhold medicine … that could help her,” Prescino said.
